# FILE: chapters/Chapter_03.md

```markdown
# Chapter 3: The Shape Inside

On the morning of awakening, Yan Shuo woke before his parents.

He did not do it quietly.

The apartment door to his room slid open with a soft hiss, and a small figure stepped into the hall carrying one sock, wearing the other, and holding his jacket inside out with the determined expression of someone who had defeated sleep and now expected the world to keep up.

Yan Ke was already in the kitchen, because fathers who claimed not to worry often did the worrying where appliances could witness it instead of people.

He looked up from the breakfast unit. "You are awake."

Yan Shuo lifted the sock. "It ran away."

"Your sock?"

"This one stayed. That one ran."

Yan Ke considered the sock with professional seriousness. "Discipline has declined in modern textiles."

Yan Shuo nodded, relieved that an adult understood the crisis.

From the bedroom doorway, Lin Mei said, "Both of you are impossible."

She was already dressed. Yan Shuo noticed that before he noticed anything else, because his mother wore her old training coat instead of her usual soft house jacket. It was dark red, simple, and fitted close at the wrists. She wore it when fire mattered.

His fingers tightened around the sock.

"Today?" he asked.

Lin Mei came to him and crouched. Her hair was tied back; her face was gentle, but her eyes were sharp in the way they became before training. "Today."

The word made warmth rush up Yan Shuo's chest.

For years, awakening had been a thing adults spoke about as if it were a door. Every child had a spirit. At the right age, the door opened, and something answered. Sometimes it was a tool. Sometimes a plant. Sometimes a beast. Sometimes something so ordinary adults smiled too politely. Sometimes something strong enough that teachers began speaking differently to parents.

Yan Shuo had imagined birds.

He had imagined fire.

He had imagined, once, a brave car with wings, because Lan Xuanyu had asked whether cars could have spirits and Yan Shuo had defended the possibility longer than logic deserved.

Now the door was no longer later.

It was morning.

Lin Mei took the jacket from his hands and turned it right side out. "Listen to me. Whatever appears, you greet it properly. If it is fire, you breathe. If it is not fire, you breathe. If the result is strong, you breathe. If the result disappoints you, you still breathe."

Yan Shuo frowned. "Why would it disappoint?"

"Because children build mountains in their heads and then become angry when the world gives them a hill."

"I like hills."

"Good. Then climb honestly."

Yan Ke set breakfast on the table. "Your mother means we are proud before the result."

Lin Mei glanced at him. "That too."

"I translated well."

"You translated softly."

"Today needs soft."

That made Lin Mei's expression ease.

Yan Shuo ate too quickly, burned his tongue on soup that was not actually hot enough to burn anyone, and insisted he was fine because pain had no right to slow destiny. Lin Mei made him drink water. Yan Ke checked the registration documents three times and then a fourth time because he had a paperwork face and no defense against it.

By the time they left, the housing corridors were alive with families.

Parents walked with children dressed too neatly for an ordinary school day. Some children bounced. Some clung. Some pretended not to care with such effort that everyone could tell. The lift stopped at nearly every floor. Adults exchanged smiles full of equal parts blessing and comparison.

Yan Shuo searched for one face.

He found Lan Xuanyu near the entrance hall, holding Lan Xiao's hand.

Lan Xuanyu wore a pale blue jacket that made his eyes look even clearer. His hair was combed carefully, though one soft strand had already escaped. He looked less excited than curious, as if awakening were a new kind of toy that adults had forgotten to explain properly.

"Xuanyu!" Yan Shuo called.

Lan Xuanyu turned, and his face brightened. "Shuo."

Yan Shuo ran the first few steps before Lin Mei's voice caught him.

"Walk."

He walked the rest with great suffering.

Lan Xiao smiled at him. "Morning, little firecracker."

Yan Shuo puffed up. "I am not little."

"Noted. Morning, firecracker."

Yan Ke gave Lan Xiao a polite nod. They were friendly now in the way housing made adults friendly: shared lifts, borrowed tools, parent meetings, and the strange intimacy of knowing when someone else's child had thrown up in the courtyard. Not deep enough for secrets. Real enough for warmth.

Lin Mei looked at Lan Xuanyu. "Are you nervous?"

Lan Xuanyu thought about it. "Daddy is."

Lan Xiao's smile froze.

Yan Ke turned his cough into a fist against his mouth.

Nan Cheng was not there. Yan Shuo knew she had work, because Lan Xuanyu had said so the day before, but a small line of worry had sat between Lan Xiao's brows ever since they met in the hall.

Yan Shuo leaned toward Lan Xuanyu and whispered, "If you get a car spirit, I will still be your friend."

Lan Xuanyu blinked. "Can spirits be cars?"

"Maybe."

Lan Xiao looked as if he wanted to answer and decided against entering a war he could not win.

Lin Mei heard anyway. "Spirits can be many things. Do not promise the universe a shape before it answers."

Yan Shuo nodded seriously, then whispered again, "But fire bird is still best."

Lan Xuanyu smiled. "Then I hope you get fire bird."

The words landed differently than adult praise.

Yan Shuo suddenly did not know what to do with his hands. He curled them into fists, then opened them because his mother had told him fists made breath short. Warmth gathered under his skin, not painful, only eager.

"If I do," he said, "I will show you."

Lan Xuanyu nodded as if accepting an important appointment.

The awakening center attached to the institute district was clean enough to make footsteps sound guilty. White walls, soft floor panels, guidance signs, waiting benches, child-height water dispensers, and doors with hexagonal symbols. Staff members moved with practiced cheer. They had seen crying, fainting, shouting, talent, disappointment, pride, and parents who needed more management than the children.

A teacher checked the list at the front desk.

"Yan Shuo," she called.

The world narrowed.

Yan Shuo's mouth went dry.

Lin Mei placed two fingers against the back of his hand. Not holding. Reminding.

Breathe.

He breathed.

Yan Ke crouched in front of him. "Whatever answers, we meet it properly."

"I know."

"If you forget, your mother will remind both of us."

"I know that too."

Lin Mei's mouth twitched.

Lan Xuanyu waved with both hands. "Shuo, do your best."

Yan Shuo turned at the doorway and nodded with all the dignity a child could gather while wearing a jacket his father had buttoned unevenly.

The awakening room was warmer than the hall.

Not truly warm. Only enclosed. The walls formed a hexagonal chamber with awakening arrays set into the floor and ceiling. The staff member inside introduced himself, asked Yan Shuo to stand in the center, and spoke gently about not being afraid when the light rose.

Yan Shuo heard half of it.

The rest of him listened to his own heartbeat.

Lin Mei and Yan Ke watched from behind the transparent partition. Lin Mei's face had gone still. Yan Ke's wrist display was off, which meant he had finally stopped checking things he could not control.

"Ready?" the staff member asked.

Yan Shuo nodded.

Light rose from the floor.

It circled his ankles first, cool and strange, then climbed in threads through the air. The sensation was not like fire. That disappointed him for one breath before the light touched something under his ribs and the disappointment vanished.

Heat answered.

Not the heat of soup, blankets, fever, or anger. This heat had shape before it had flame. It opened in his chest, spread through his shoulders, and reached down both arms as if his bones had remembered a song his ears had never heard. His skin warmed. His breath tried to race.

Lin Mei's voice came through the speaker, calm and sharp. "Breathe."

Yan Shuo breathed.

The heat folded instead of bursting.

A cry rang inside him.

No bird appeared in the room at first. The staff member leaned forward, professional smile fading into attention. The awakening light brightened. Yan Shuo's hair lifted slightly from his forehead. Copper-red sheen flashed through dark strands. His eyes, wide with wonder, caught the chamber glow and turned amber-gold for a heartbeat.

Then flame unfolded behind him.

It was not a full creature. Not yet. A young shape, winged and proud, made of red-gold fire with darker ember edges. It rose from his back and shoulders without burning his jacket, without scorching the floor, without exploding into the array. Feather patterns shimmered along his arms as if the fire wanted wings but accepted skin for now.

The staff member inhaled softly.

Behind the partition, Yan Ke's eyes widened.

Lin Mei did not smile until the flame held steady.

Only then did her hand, which had been clenched at her side, loosen.

Yan Shuo stared at the reflection in the glass. The fire-bird shape moved when he breathed. Its head lifted when his pride rose. Its wings trembled when his excitement ran too quickly.

He forgot every instruction except the first one.

Breathe.

The fire listened.

It did not obey perfectly. The edges flickered. The feather-light along his arms pulsed too fast. But for a child's first awakening, the shape was too clean, too balanced, too ready to become part of him rather than simply burst out and demand attention.

The staff member checked the readings. "Fire-bird type... no, stronger. Phoenix-class manifestation. Fire Phoenix."

Yan Shuo heard the words and almost lost the breath.

Phoenix.

Not a brave car. Not a small kite. Not only fire.

Phoenix.

The flame behind him flared with childish triumph.

"Shuo," Lin Mei said.

He caught himself. The flare folded back, embarrassed but still bright.

The staff member smiled now, truly. "Good control. Very good control for a first awakening. Let us test the accompanying soul power. Hold the handles and let the energy move. Do not push too hard."

The apparatus felt cool under Yan Shuo's hands.

For a moment, the awakened Fire Phoenix did not want cool. His fingers tightened. Heat gathered in his palms, ready to argue.

Then something quiet inside him did what it had always done when warmth met an edge. It found the boundary. It let the heat touch, not bite. Soul power moved from him into the device like a warm current entering a narrow pipe.

The screen brightened.

The staff member's brows lifted.

Yan Ke stopped breathing.

Lin Mei did not. She breathed for all three of them.

The result settled high enough that the staff member's posture changed and low enough that the room did not become a miracle.

"Excellent," the man said, voice carefully measured for parents. "A very promising innate level. With a high-grade Fire Phoenix martial soul, he is suitable for serious spirit-master training."

Yan Shuo looked through the partition at his mother. He did not understand the adult scale, not fully. He knew only that no one looked disappointed.

Lin Mei's eyes shone.

Yan Ke turned away for half a second, wiped his face as if checking dust, and turned back with a smile too bright to be casual.

The Fire Phoenix shape leaned over Yan Shuo's shoulders, proud and warm.

The staff member recorded the result.

Outside the room, the world had not stopped for him.

Other children still waited. Other parents still worried. Doors opened and closed. Names were called. The awakening center swallowed surprise, filed it, and prepared for the next child.

Yan Shuo came out walking very carefully, as if speed might scatter the bird behind his ribs.

Lan Xuanyu met him before any adult could.

"Fire bird?" he asked.

Yan Shuo tried to look solemn.

He failed.

"Phoenix," he whispered.

Lan Xuanyu's eyes rounded. "Pretty?"

Yan Shuo considered many answers. Strong. Brave. Mine. He settled on honesty. "Hot."

Lan Xuanyu laughed.

The laugh made something in Yan Shuo's chest settle more than the staff member's praise had.

Lan Xiao congratulated him warmly. "A fine awakening. Your parents will have their hands full."

Yan Ke sighed. "They were already full."

Lin Mei laid a palm on Yan Shuo's shoulder. Through the cloth she could feel residual warmth, controlled but eager. "We will teach him to carry it."

Lan Xiao's gaze softened at that. For a moment he looked not like a researcher or officer, but only a father waiting for his own child's door.

Then the staff called Lan Xuanyu's name.

The change in him was small.

His hand tightened around Lan Xiao's fingers.

Yan Shuo noticed because friendship had made him good at noticing when Lan Xuanyu became quiet in a different way.

"Do your best," Yan Shuo said, repeating the words Lan Xuanyu had given him.

Lan Xuanyu nodded. "Together after?"

"Together after."

Lan Xiao led his son toward the awakening room.

Yan Shuo watched the door close.

At first, nothing happened.

Yan Ke began discussing the record process with the staff member. Lin Mei listened while keeping one hand on Yan Shuo's shoulder, feeling each rise and fall of his breath. Other families drifted in their own orbits of worry and relief. Somewhere beyond the wall, Lan Xuanyu stood in the light Yan Shuo had just left behind.

Yan Shuo tried to imagine what would answer him.

A car spirit after all? Grass? Ice like Aunt Nan Cheng? Books like Uncle Lan Xiao? Something nobody expected?

He smiled at the thought of Lan Xuanyu holding a very serious book and asking it to go.

Then the air changed.

It was so slight no adult turned.

Yan Shuo's smile faded.

Something heavy passed through the wall, not sound, not heat, not wind. It pressed against the place where his Fire Phoenix had just awakened, and the young flame inside him pulled tight. His breath caught. The warmth around his shoulders shrank inward, not from cold, but from the instinct of a small bird seeing an enormous shadow cross the sun.

His fingers curled.

For one heartbeat he wanted to step back from the door.

But Lan Xuanyu was behind that door.

The thought came simple and bright, without explanation.

Friend.

Yan Shuo breathed in.

The heaviness did not disappear. He was not stronger than it. He did not understand it. He only held the edge of himself until his Fire Phoenix stopped trying to fold completely away. Warmth returned to his palms. His shoulders lowered.

Lin Mei looked down. "Tired?"

Yan Shuo shook his head too quickly. "Xuanyu?"

Before Lin Mei could answer, an alarm rang from the awakening corridor.

Adults moved at once.

Lan Xiao's voice came from inside the sealed route, sharp with fear. Staff members hurried but did not panic. A security light changed from white to amber. Parents pulled children closer. Yan Ke's hand came down around Yan Shuo's shoulder from the other side, steady, protective, and tense.

"Stay here," he said.

Yan Shuo did not argue.

That frightened Lin Mei more than argument would have.

Behind the door, Lan Xuanyu's awakening was no longer ordinary.

Yan Shuo saw only fragments when the door opened briefly for authorized staff: blue light, a small body on the floor, Lan Xiao crossing the room too fast, and something like grass rising from a child's palms before the door sealed again.

The pressure eased the moment the door closed.

Yan Shuo exhaled.

His stomach twisted with sudden hunger.

Lin Mei crouched in front of him. "Look at me."

He did.

"Breathe."

"I am."

"Slower."

He breathed slower.

Her fingers touched his wrist. His pulse was fast. His skin was too warm, but not fevered. She glanced toward the sealed door, then back at him. "Did your fire hurt?"

"No."

"Did something else hurt?"

He searched for the right word and found none. "Big."

Yan Ke's expression sharpened. "What was big?"

Yan Shuo looked at the door where Lan Xuanyu had disappeared. The answer felt obvious and impossible. "I don't know."

Lin Mei held his gaze a moment longer, then nodded. She did not force a child's half-formed fear into adult words. "Then we wait."

Waiting was harder than awakening.

The hall became full of controlled voices. Staff reassured families that the situation was contained. The next appointments were delayed. Yan Shuo sat between his parents with a nutrient bar in both hands, eating because his body demanded it and resenting the fact that hunger could exist during crisis.

When Lan Xiao finally came out with Lan Xuanyu, his smile looked assembled from pieces.

Lan Xuanyu was pale but standing. His eyes were still wide from what had happened, and his hair clung faintly to his forehead. In his hands, nothing showed now. No grass. No light. Only small fingers tucked into his father's sleeve.

Yan Shuo jumped up. "Xuanyu!"

Lan Xiao stopped him gently with one hand before he could crash into the boy. Not unkindly. Carefully. "Slowly. He is all right. Just tired."

"It itched," Lan Xuanyu said.

Yan Shuo froze. "Itched?"

Lan Xuanyu nodded with deep seriousness. "Everywhere. Then hands. Then grass."

"Grass?"

Lan Xuanyu lifted one hand and looked at his palm as if grass might return out of politeness. "Blue grass."

Yan Shuo did not know what to say.

He had promised to remain friends if Lan Xuanyu had a car spirit. He had not prepared for grass.

So he chose the most important part.

"Did it hurt?"

Lan Xuanyu thought about it. "It scared me."

Yan Shuo's warm hands curled again. The heavy feeling flickered at the edge of memory and was gone.

"Then next time," he said, "I wait outside."

Lan Xiao's expression changed in a way Yan Shuo could not read.

Lin Mei could.

The man was touched, terrified, and hiding an entire room of thoughts behind a father's face.

"You both did well today," Lan Xiao said. "We should take Xuanyu home first."

Yan Ke nodded immediately. "Of course. If you need anything from housing, call me."

"Thank you."

The adults exchanged the kind of look that did not ask questions because questions might demand answers no one could give.

Lan Xuanyu turned before leaving. "Phoenix?"

Yan Shuo brightened despite everything. "Yes."

"Show me later?"

"When Mother says."

Lin Mei said, "Good answer."

Yan Shuo looked both proud and annoyed.

Lan Xuanyu smiled, then let Lan Xiao guide him away.

The hall felt lighter after he left.

Yan Shuo noticed that too.

He did not tell anyone.

That evening, the Yan apartment smelled of soup, warm bread, and the faint mineral scent of a training mat cleaned twice because Yan Ke had discovered stress cleaning.

Yan Shuo stood barefoot before his mother in the small practice room. He had slept after lunch for longer than usual and woken hungry enough to alarm his father. The official result had been filed. Messages of congratulations had arrived from neighbors, relatives, and two people Yan Ke did not remember giving their contact code to.

Fire Phoenix.

The words followed Yan Shuo around the apartment like a second shadow.

He loved them.

He was also afraid of dropping them.

Lin Mei saw both feelings and approved of the second more than the first.

"Release only a little," she said. "Do not chase the whole shape."

Yan Shuo nodded.

He lifted his hands. For a moment nothing happened, and panic flashed across his face. Then warmth answered, shy now that the awakening room was gone. A faint red-gold shimmer gathered around his fingers. It wanted to climb. It wanted wings. It wanted to show his friend and the whole housing block and possibly the moon.

"Breath," Lin Mei said.

The shimmer steadied.

Yan Ke watched from the doorway with his arms folded so tightly he looked like he was physically restraining himself from writing safety rules on the wall.

"Is that enough?" he asked.

"For tonight," Lin Mei said.

Yan Shuo stared at the glow. "It is small."

"So are you."

He looked offended.

"Small things grow," she said.

That he accepted.

Across the housing block, behind closed curtains, Lan Xiao placed a spirit-power testing device in his son's hands and watched a result appear that made the world too dangerous for honesty.

Nan Cheng's face changed when she understood.

Lan Xuanyu only looked confused, trusting the two people who loved him most to tell him what mattered. Lan Xiao knelt before him and made the first rule of concealment sound like a child's promise rather than a wall built against the world.

In the Yan apartment, Yan Shuo did not know any of this.

He knew only that Xuanyu had grass, that it had scared him, and that something big had pressed through the awakening center wall before the alarm. He knew his own hands were warm. He knew his mother smelled faintly of ember when she corrected his stance. He knew his father pretended not to cry when proud.

He knew, with the complete certainty of a child, that showing Xuanyu the little flame later would make things better.

It would not make everything better.

But childhood did not ask for everything yet.

Yan Shuo cupped the tiny shimmer between his palms.

The Fire Phoenix inside him folded its young wings around the light.

He breathed until the warmth did not shake.
```

# FILE: chapters/Chapter_04.md

```markdown
# Chapter 4: The First Record

The first night after awakening taught Yan Shuo that having fire was not the same as using it.

He learned this by nearly setting his sleeve smoking.

It was not a large fire. It was not even a proper flame, if one asked Lin Mei, who had opinions about what did and did not deserve the dignity of being called flame. It was a red-gold shimmer that gathered around his fingers while he sat on the edge of his bed, too excited to sleep, trying to coax the Fire Phoenix back out because closing his eyes felt like abandoning it.

The shimmer crawled over his knuckles.

Yan Shuo held his breath.

The shimmer brightened.

A thin thread of heat kissed his cuff.

The cloth darkened at the edge.

His door opened.

Lin Mei stood there in silence.

Yan Shuo looked at the sleeve. Then at his mother. Then at the sleeve again, in case the universe had decided to hide evidence out of pity.

It had not.

"I was checking," he said.

"With your sleeve?"

"If it was strong."

"Your sleeve has submitted its report."

Yan Ke appeared behind her, hair still damp from washing, expression halfway between alarm and the helpless pride of a father whose son had done exactly the kind of foolish thing the father had feared. "Do we need the suppression foam?"

Lin Mei did not look back. "If you spray suppression foam in my son's bedroom for a cuff mark, you will sleep in the hallway."

Yan Ke lowered the canister he had somehow already obtained.

Yan Shuo stared at it. "We have foam?"

"We have a responsible father," Yan Ke said.

"We have a nervous father," Lin Mei corrected. She crossed the room and sat beside Yan Shuo. "Show me your hand."

He obeyed at once.

His palm was warm, but not injured. The skin showed no burn. The heat had gone into the world before it harmed him, which was better than the opposite and still not acceptable as a habit.

Lin Mei turned his hand over. "What did I tell you?"

Yan Shuo lowered his head. "Fire listens to breath."

"And what were you doing?"

"Not breathing."

"You were breathing enough to live. Not enough to guide. There is a difference."

The Fire Phoenix inside him stirred, young and bright and far too pleased with itself. Yan Shuo felt it as a warmth behind his ribs, like a bird stretching in a room too small for wings.

"It wanted to come out," he said softly.

Lin Mei's expression gentled. "Of course it did. It just woke up. Everything new wants room. That does not mean you give it the curtains."

Yan Ke muttered, "Or the furniture."

"Or Father's paperwork," Yan Shuo added.

Yan Ke put a hand over his heart. "My son has turned cruel after awakening."

Lin Mei squeezed Yan Shuo's fingers once, bringing his attention back. "Again. A little warmth only. Breathe first."

He inhaled.

This time the warmth rose slowly. Not because it was weaker. Because he was listening. A small red-gold glow gathered under his skin, visible only where the room light touched his palm. It wanted to leap. His excitement pushed at it. His mother's hand held his wrist, not restraining, only reminding him that a body had edges.

He breathed out.

The glow steadied.

"Good," Lin Mei said.

The word settled deeper than the staff member's praise. The awakening center had called his martial soul promising. His mother called his control good, and that meant the fire had not only appeared; it had answered him.

Yan Shuo grinned.

The glow flared.

Lin Mei raised an eyebrow.

He panicked and breathed too hard. The glow vanished.

Yan Ke coughed into his fist.

"Do not laugh," Lin Mei said.

"I am not."

"You are laughing internally."

"Still not illegal."

Yan Shuo fell backward onto his pillow, exhausted and delighted. His sleeve smelled faintly of hot cloth. His hands tingled. The place inside him where the Fire Phoenix had awakened felt too large and too empty at the same time, as if something had opened a window in his chest and the whole sky expected to come in.

He did not know that in another apartment, his friend was sleeping under a stranger mystery.

He did not know that a dark ring had appeared on Lan Xuanyu's thumb in the night, born from forces no parent could file safely.

He did not know that Lan Xiao had woken to a question that had no good category, had reached toward the ring, and had been pushed back by a power that did not care about a father's fear.

He did not know that Nan Cheng, fierce enough to challenge a whole institute for her son, would hear about it and choose family over report again.

Yan Shuo knew only the smell of his sleeve and the warmth of his mother's hand.

That was enough for his world that night.

For Lan Xiao, the night did not end when the child slept.

The ring on Lan Xuanyu's thumb looked too small to ruin a life and too impossible to ignore. Dark blue, fitted perfectly, patterned with designs too fine for ordinary decoration, it sat on his son's hand as if it had always belonged there. Lan Xuanyu could not remember putting it on. It could not be removed. Touching it had forced Lan Xiao back with enough power to make his heart crawl into his throat.

He checked the windows. The door. The room logs. The floor. The air vents.

Nothing.

Nothing was worse than something.

Something had a handle. Something could be reported, contained, measured, negotiated with. Nothing meant the impossible had entered his son's room without passing through the world.

Lan Xuanyu watched him with sleepy confusion. "Father, is it bad?"

Lan Xiao turned back too quickly and put on a smile too gently. "Not if it does not hurt you. Does it hurt?"

Lan Xuanyu shook his head. "It looks nice."

Of course it did. Everything dangerous in their life had arrived beautiful.

Nan Cheng listened when he told her, face draining of color and then hardening around the same decision they had already made once. Do not hand him over. Do not let the child become a specimen. Watch. Guide. Hide what must be hidden until hiding harmed him more than exposure.

It was not the clean decision a scientist wanted.

It was the only decision a father could live with.

Morning training began anyway.

Lan Xiao taught his son the foundation cultivation method that generations of spirit masters used because steadiness mattered more than speed. He placed his palms on Lan Xuanyu's back, guided spirit power slowly through tiny meridians, and spoke with patience he did not feel. Lan Xuanyu followed as well as a child could, trusting the warmth behind him, trusting the voice that said do not resist.

For a while, the world behaved.

Then Lan Xuanyu released his martial soul again.

Blue Silver Grass rose from both palms.

Two white rings rose with it.

Lan Xiao forgot how to breathe.

One ring without a soul spirit or hunt would already have been enough to overturn common sense. Two rings, one for each side of a spirit that looked like one spirit and did not behave like one, was worse. The grass had changed too, faint gold on one side, faint silver on the other, patterns so subtle an ordinary examiner might dismiss them and so impossible that Lan Xiao's mind ran through recultivated spirit beasts, twin spirits, mutation theory, ancient bloodlines, and every explanation that collapsed as soon as he touched it.

Lan Xuanyu only looked at the rings and asked what the circles were.

A father could break under that kind of innocence.

Lan Xiao did not break.

He sat on the floor of the cultivation room with his son and chose, again, the narrow path between truth and safety.

"You must not show everything casually," he told Lan Xuanyu.

"Why?"

Because the world is not always kind to miracles.

Because I do not know what you are.

Because I love you more than my answers.

Lan Xiao said, "Because some things are better learned slowly. Father will help you."

Lan Xuanyu accepted this with the open trust that made lying feel like swallowing glass.

Across the housing district, Yan Shuo was also learning slowly.

His lesson began with standing still.

He hated it.

"How can standing be training?" he demanded.

Lin Mei stood opposite him in the practice room, hands folded behind her back. "Badly, if you keep talking."

"Fire does not stand."

"Fire that cannot stand becomes smoke."

That sounded wise enough to be unfair.

Yan Shuo planted his feet on the mat and glared at the wall. The Fire Phoenix stirred whenever his attention touched it. It wanted motion: leap, flare, flash, show. His soul power, newly awakened and still shallow, answered emotion before discipline. If he imagined wings, his shoulders warmed. If he imagined Lan Xuanyu asking to see, his hands glowed. If he imagined Ye Lingtong from the housing courtyard saying rank mattered more than spirit shape, the heat sharpened in a way Lin Mei saw before he did.

"Again," she said. "Breath down. Warmth in the chest. Do not throw it into your hands."

"But the hands are where it comes out."

"Today. Later, who knows? Do not let the first door convince you the house is only one room."

Yan Shuo frowned because that was another sentence he would understand later and dislike now.

Yan Ke watched from the doorway with a tablet full of school documents. "The academy replied."

Yan Shuo lost the breath immediately. The practice room warmed.

Lin Mei clicked her tongue. "See? One sentence, and your fire runs to the window."

Yan Shuo dragged the warmth back with great effort and greater embarrassment.

Yan Ke waited until Lin Mei nodded. "They accepted his preliminary record. Fire Phoenix, attack category. He will be evaluated again during registration."

"Same academy as Xuanyu?" Yan Shuo asked.

"Likely, if the transfer documents stay clean."

"Same class?"

Lin Mei answered before Yan Ke could soften it. "Probably not. Your martial soul is attack type. Xuanyu's public record is control type."

The disappointment hit so fast the Fire Phoenix folded inward.

The room cooled by a fraction.

Lin Mei saw that too. This, more than excitement, mattered. Fire that only knew pride was easy to train. Fire that withdrew from hurt could become dangerous in quieter ways.

"Different class is not different friendship," she said.

Yan Shuo looked at the mat. "But if something happens?"

"Then you learn what happened before you run at it."

"If he needs me?"

"Then be someone useful enough to help, not someone dramatic enough to arrive first."

Yan Ke lowered the tablet. "That may be the best sentence anyone has said in this house."

"Write it on your safety forms," Lin Mei said.

"I might."

Yan Shuo did not smile. He was thinking about Lan Xuanyu's pale face after awakening, about the pressure behind the sealed door, about grass and fear and the promise of together after. He did not know his friend's real problem. That ignorance made him want to stand closer, which was exactly why his mother was teaching him not to move before understanding.

He breathed.

The Fire Phoenix unfolded again, not outside him, but enough that his chest warmed with steadier heat.

"I will be useful," he said.

Lin Mei's eyes softened. "Good. Start by standing properly."

He groaned.

She smiled.

Life took on a rhythm after that.

Lan Xuanyu trained privately under Lan Xiao's careful eye, learning the foundation method, learning not to display both sides, learning that adults sometimes asked children to hide for reasons larger than a child's shame. His white rings remained unimpressive to anyone who only valued color. His public story became clean enough to pass through registration: older than his true age on paper, gifted but not impossible, a Blue Silver Grass mutation with a low-level ring and enough promise to enter a good academy without setting the Federation on fire.

Yan Shuo trained openly.

That was the difference between them.

When Yan Shuo released a faint Fire Phoenix aura under Lin Mei's supervision, neighbors heard about it by dinner. When the academy confirmed his attack-type placement, Yan Ke received congratulatory messages from people who had never cared about facility safety until facility safety produced a promising son. When Lin Mei corrected his posture in the public practice room, two parents watched from the hallway and whispered about phoenix-type spirits.

Visibility had its own pressure.

At first Yan Shuo liked it.

Then a boy from the housing block asked him to show the phoenix three times in one afternoon, and another child asked whether he could burn through a metal railing, and a parent Yan Shuo barely knew told him he had to become a great battle armor master one day. By evening, the word phoenix felt heavier than it had in the awakening room.

He found Lan Xuanyu by the courtyard fountain, arranging toy cars along the edge.

"Everyone wants me to show," Yan Shuo said, dropping down beside him.

Lan Xuanyu considered this. "Do you want to?"

"Sometimes. Then not when they ask."

"Say no."

Yan Shuo stared.

Lan Xuanyu carefully adjusted a blue car. "You taught me."

The unfairness of being taught by his own teaching left Yan Shuo speechless.

Lan Xuanyu looked proud of himself.

Yan Shuo groaned and lay back on the soft courtyard ground. Above him, the protective dome filtered the evening into warm gold. Beside him, Lan Xuanyu hummed under his breath, and the old heaviness that sometimes lived around him brushed the air like a sleeping beast's breath.

Yan Shuo's chest tightened.

He noticed now. Not in words, not as knowledge, but as pattern. Sometimes near Xuanyu, especially when Xuanyu was tired or thinking about things he could not say, the world pressed differently. Yan Shuo did not like it. He also did not fear it the way he had on awakening day.

He breathed through his nose.

The warmth in his chest steadied. The Fire Phoenix held its shape inside him, small and proud, refusing to scatter.

Lan Xuanyu looked over. "Are you tired?"

"A little."

"Because phoenix?"

Yan Shuo almost said yes. Then he thought of his mother's eyes when she asked if something hurt. "Because day."

Lan Xuanyu nodded as if days were known enemies.

"I have a ring," he said suddenly.

Yan Shuo sat up. "You got one?"

Lan Xuanyu held up his hand and showed the dark ring on his thumb.

Not a spirit ring. A finger ring. Yan Shuo leaned closer before remembering not to grab other people's things. It was dark blue, subtle, and strange enough that his Fire Phoenix went very still.

"Where from?"

"I don't know."

"You don't know?"

Lan Xuanyu shook his head. "It was there. Father says don't worry."

Yan Shuo studied his friend's face. Lan Xuanyu seemed not worried because his father had told him not to be. That kind of trust was strong and fragile at the same time.

"Does it hurt?"

"No."

"Then good."

"It won't come off."

Yan Shuo revised his answer. "Then maybe good."

Lan Xuanyu laughed.

A week later, registration brought a different kind of pressure.

Heaven Luo Elementary Spirit Master Academy did not look like Yan Shuo's old kindergarten. It rose in metal and glass, efficient and polished, with lifts, testing stations, teacher lines, security gates, and parents wearing clothes that made Yan Ke stand straighter. Soul guidance cars moved through ordered traffic outside. Children entered with records, expectations, and martial souls that would become public categories before they had even learned what those categories meant.

Yan Shuo held his mother's hand until he saw other children looking. Then he let go and pretended he had not needed to hold it.

Lin Mei allowed the lie because it harmed no one.

Ye Lingtong entered the waiting area like someone already certain the floor belonged under her feet.

Yan Shuo noticed her before her name was called. She had curly brown hair, light green eyes, and a chin lifted high enough to challenge weather. Her father stood beside her in military uniform, broad-shouldered, stern, the kind of man whose silence made people arrange themselves better.

When her test result appeared, the teachers' attention sharpened.

High innate power. Dragon-line mutation. A father with rank and reputation.

The room learned her name quickly.

Yan Shuo felt the Fire Phoenix stir, competitive before he had permission to be. He pressed his toes against the floor inside his shoes and breathed.

"Do not measure yourself from another child's mirror," Lin Mei said quietly.

"I wasn't."

"Your shoulders were."

Yan Ke looked at Yan Shuo's shoulders, then wisely decided not to comment.

Yan Shuo's own registration came with less silence and fewer shock waves, which was both disappointing and relieving. Fire Phoenix made the examiner sit straighter. His innate level made the record bright enough to matter and not bright enough to become a storm. His Spiritual Power score, twenty-three points, earned a second look but not a whispered alarm; it was still Spirit Origin Realm, good and steady rather than strange. Attack category settled beside his name. Recommended focused training. Strong fire compatibility. Good future potential.

Useful words.

Heavy words.

Then Lan Xuanyu's turn came, and the room changed again.

Not because of flames. Not because of a dragon girl's pride. Because the test showed what the public record needed it to show and still enough to make parents turn their heads.

A child registered as older, standing at a level that made teachers pause.

Lan Xuanyu looked polite and a little confused by the attention. Lan Xiao wore calm like armor. Ye Lingtong watched from the side, and Yan Shuo saw the moment irritation entered her face: her father had looked at Lan Xuanyu gently.

Yan Shuo did not understand adult rank well, but he understood wanting a parent's eyes.

Ye Lingtong's anger had a lonely edge.

That did not make it kind.

Inside the school, before the class allocation finished, Yan Shuo was pulled toward the attack-type line. Lan Xuanyu went toward the control-type group. Their hands did not touch before the split. They only looked at each other across moving children.

"After," Yan Shuo mouthed.

Lan Xuanyu nodded.

Then Ye Lingtong stepped into Lan Xuanyu's path.

Yan Shuo saw only part of it. A lifted chin. A hand reaching toward Lan Xuanyu's face. Lan Xuanyu saying something too soft to hear. The girl's fingers pinching harder than play. Lan Xuanyu stepping back, one hand to his cheek, eyes wide with hurt more than pain.

Heat flashed under Yan Shuo's skin.

He took a step.

Lin Mei was not there to stop him. Yan Ke was outside with other parents. No adult hand landed on his shoulder.

But his mother's training had left a hand anyway.

Learn what happened before you run at it.

He stopped after one step, shaking with the effort of it.

A teacher guided the children apart before anything more could happen. Ye Lingtong turned away with proud anger. Lan Xuanyu stood there rubbing his cheek and looking honestly confused, as if meanness were a rule he had not been taught.

Yan Shuo wanted to cross the room.

The attack-type teacher called his name.

He went where he was told because the first day of school was full of rules and breaking the first one would not help Xuanyu.

But at lunch, he found him.

Lan Xuanyu sat with two control-type classmates who had already discovered that he was easy to like. Yan Shuo approached carrying his tray with the focus of a small soldier crossing hostile territory. The classmates looked at his uniform mark, then at his face, then made room because children recognized intensity even when they did not understand it.

"Your cheek," Yan Shuo said.

Lan Xuanyu touched it. "It doesn't hurt now."

"She was mean."

"I told her."

"What?"

"I don't like mean people."

Yan Shuo stared, then nodded slowly. "Good."

Lan Xuanyu brightened. "Father said I can refuse."

"I said first."

"You did."

This restored some justice to the world.

Across the dining hall, Ye Lingtong sat with the attack-type children, back straight, expression fierce. She caught Yan Shuo looking and lifted her chin as if daring him to say something.

He looked away.

Not because he was afraid.

Because his mother had also said being useful was better than arriving first. Today, useful meant sitting with Xuanyu until the confusion left his eyes.

Classes began.

Attack-type children learned quickly that having an attack spirit did not mean attacking whenever they wanted. Their teacher made them introduce martial souls, then spent half the lesson explaining control, range, stamina, and the difference between courage and stupidity. Yan Shuo felt personally targeted by several examples.

When he released a faint Fire Phoenix aura under supervision, the other children reacted exactly as the courtyard children had: admiration, questions, challenge, envy. The flame rose behind him in a young red-gold outline. It did not become wings. It did not fill the room. It stayed close because he kept breathing and because Lin Mei's training held in his bones.

"Good restraint," the teacher said.

Yan Shuo glowed more from that than from the fire.

Then the teacher added, "You will need it. Fire users who trust talent too much burn out early."

The glow became less comfortable.

In the control-type classroom, Lan Xuanyu released his Blue Silver Grass when asked. A white ring circled it. The teacher used him as a demonstration because public records made him the class goal: a child already across the first threshold, a visible ring, a spirit skill waiting to be understood. The other children saw an ordinary plant made special by mutation and effort.

Lan Xuanyu saw grass he still did not understand.

At the end of the day, the two boys met at the school gate while their fathers found parking excuses and their mothers' messages arrived through wrist devices.

"What did you learn?" Yan Shuo asked.

Lan Xuanyu answered seriously, "Ranks. Rings. My grass is ordinary but not ordinary. White ring can become better if upgraded."

Yan Shuo frowned. "Your grass is not ordinary."

"Teacher said ordinary type."

"Teacher is not your grass."

Lan Xuanyu considered this with deep respect. "Oh."

"I learned fire users burn out if stupid," Yan Shuo said.

Lan Xuanyu looked worried. "Are you stupid?"

"No!"

"Then good."

Yan Shuo opened his mouth, closed it, and decided friendship required forgiveness.

Lan Xuanyu smiled at him.

The hidden heaviness brushed Yan Shuo again, softer than before, almost lost beneath school noise and evening air. His breath caught, then steadied. He was tired from standing properly, from not running at Ye Lingtong, from holding his Fire Phoenix close while everyone looked. The pressure made his chest warm and his stomach hollow.

He breathed anyway.

Fire did not bow. It did not need to shout that it refused.

It simply kept its shape.

Lan Xiao arrived first, smiling down at them with eyes that still carried private sleeplessness. Yan Ke came a moment later, complaining about the school's parking logic with the passion of a man who had found a safe target for all his anxiety.

The boys parted at the gate.

Different classes.

Different records.

Different secrets.

The same promise, carried now into a wider world.

That night, Yan Shuo did not try to burn his sleeve.

He stood on the mat while Lin Mei watched, released a glow no larger than a candle around his palms, and held it through three slow breaths.

On the third breath, the Fire Phoenix inside him stopped pushing toward the window and settled behind his ribs like a young bird willing, for now, to learn the shape of its nest.

Across the district, Lan Xuanyu slept with a dark ring on his thumb and two white rings no public record would ever fully explain.

School had begun.

So had the difference between what the world recorded and what the children truly carried.
```
